text:
The Enterprise Chamber of the Court of Appeal in Amsterdam's 29 September 2026 ruling cleared Keurig Dr Pepper (via Kodiak BidCo) to proceed with a squeeze-out of remaining JDE Peet's shareholders at EUR 31.85 per share plus statutory interest. KDP has set 16 October 2026, 15:00 CET as the deadline for voluntary share transfer, after which untransferred shares convert by operation of law and the purchase price is deposited with the Dutch consignment office. This closes out the minority stake following the 97.75% position KDP already holds.

Several EU regulatory deadlines converge this period. On EUDR, the Commission's 21 August 2026 corrigendum specifically clarified supply-chain classification for coffee roasters and decaffeinators ahead of the 30 December 2026 enforcement deadline — directly relevant to JDE Peet's processing operations. PPWR's Declaration of Conformity obligations took effect 12 August 2026, with the Commission publishing updated FAQ guidance (26 new, 7 updated Q&As) only nine days earlier and recommending a supportive rather than punitive enforcement posture from national authorities. Separately, the Netherlands' 27 September 2026 implementation of the EU's Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition directive tightens substantiation requirements for environmental marketing claims and bars unverified eco-labels, applying immediately to food and beverage packaging; this suggests a review of sustainability claims on Dutch-market packaging may be warranted.

On the competitive side, KDP continues building leadership for its planned early-2027 separation into "Beverage Co." and "Global Coffee Co." Russ Torres, formerly President and COO of Kimberly-Clark, was named CEO of the future Global Coffee Co., effective 3 November 2026, tasked with integrating KDP's and JDE Peet's coffee operations ahead of the split and reporting to KDP CEO Tim Cofer. This follows the board's earlier addition of Aaron Alt, whose appointment was explicitly framed around the two-company separation.

On supply chain, an El Niño-linked drought pushed Central American arabica premiums to roughly three-year highs, directly affecting input costs for Jacobs, L'OR, Douwe Egberts, Kenco and Moccona. Separately, shipments from Colombia's Buenaventura port — a major coffee export hub — have only partially resumed after disruptions, coinciding with a sharp 13 August drop in coffee futures (New York December contract down 2.2%, London November down 2.9%), underscoring continued volatility in sourcing markets.
